comparison: Both evaluate the same claims (C11, C13-C15, C51, C59) about model accuracy and regulator discovery. OpenEval finds the quantitative results and visual predictions sufficient support. Peer reviewers raise critical concerns about circular reasoning, noting conclusions are drawn from training data rather than blind tests or proper cross-validation, creating uncertainty about validity.

Both evaluate C12 regarding dorsoventral information encoded in anteroposterior regulators. OpenEval finds empirical support in visual predictions. Peer reviewers did not challenge this finding, suggesting implicit acceptance of this novel insight about information sufficiency.

Both address C16-C19 about concentration-dependent dual regulation of Hb. OpenEval finds the quadratic model provides biologically plausible resolution of the paradox. Peer reviewers question the methodology of manipulating input signals without re-optimizing model coefficients, undermining confidence in the dual regulation interpretation.

Both evaluate C20-C22 regarding mutant predictions matching experimental results. OpenEval considers these independent validation of the model. Peer reviewers criticize the perturbation simulation approach, stating models should be re-optimized when inputs change and comparisons should use blind tests, not training data.

Both assess C39-C41 about quadratic models capturing fine-scale spatial features in hb misexpression. OpenEval finds strong validation in detailed visual comparisons. Peer reviewers apply their methodological critique about re-optimization and blind testing to these predictions, creating uncertainty about claimed accuracy.

Both evaluate C42-C47 regarding high-level mechanistic conclusions about regulation. OpenEval finds collective model success supports these inferences. Peer reviewers question whether novel testable predictions emerge and raise concerns about statistical validation methods and variable selection, leaving mechanistic conclusions uncertain.

Both address C48-C50 about Hb's concentration-dependent dual regulation mechanism. OpenEval finds support in model performance and biological precedent. Peer reviewers' methodological concerns about perturbation simulations and lack of explicit testable predictions undermine confidence in this mechanistic interpretation.

OpenEval R7 addresses C23-C30 about variable selection and model comparison. Peer R5 covers overlapping claims (C23, C26-C30). OpenEval finds multiple lines of evidence favor the quadratic model. Peer reviewers request investigation of variable correlations, suggest alternative methods like stepwise logistic regression, and raise validation concerns about the variable selection approach.

OpenEval R9 addresses C35-C38 (experimental context from literature). Peer R6 includes these claims plus C33-C34 (model predictions). OpenEval supports the accurate reporting of experimental observations. Peer reviewers criticize the perturbation methodology for kni elimination predictions, undermining confidence in both linear model success and quadratic model explanations.

Both evaluate overlapping claims about kni perturbations (C33-C34 shared). OpenEval notes discrepancy requiring additional assumptions for quadratic model reconciliation. Peer reviewers apply fundamental methodological critique about re-optimization when inputs change. Both find uncertainty, though for somewhat different reasons.

Minimal overlap (C54 only). OpenEval R1 broadly supports dataset documentation and methods. Peer R10 specifically questions the single time point choice (C54), suggesting extension to earlier developmental stages to test model stability, indicating this methodological choice is a limitation.

OpenEval R2 addresses C4-C10 about established knowledge of eve regulation and prior work context. No corresponding peer review evaluation found; these background claims were not specifically challenged by reviewers.
OpenEval R13 addresses C52 about limitations of previous modeling efforts. No corresponding peer review evaluation found; reviewers did not specifically challenge the characterization of prior work.

OpenEval R14 addresses C57-C58 about model prediction of cross-regulatory effects validated by literature. No corresponding peer review evaluation found; this additional validation point was not specifically discussed by reviewers.
